51:- **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `VulnerabilityRepository.recomputeExceptedAll()` was a single `UPDATE vulnerability v JOIN asset a … SET v.excepted = CASE WHEN EXISTS(…)` **with no WHERE clause**. It took exclusive row locks on every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M in production) and, through its correlated subquery, read locks on `vulnerability_exception` — holding both for the entire 53–180s transaction. Every concurrent writer to either table then blocked until lock-wait-timeout: bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike imports, per-asset recomputes. `DeadlockRetry` absorbed the failure, which is exactly why it stayed hidden — but the *other* operation still paid the full timeout first, observed as ~40s per `delete_all_vulnerability_exceptions` in both E2E runs, contending with "Async full excepted recompute complete: 1824736 rows in 53481 ms". Fix: `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` drives the recompute as bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through the new `recomputeExceptedForIdRange(afterId, throughId)`, each in its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Lock hold per transaction drops from minutes to milliseconds, so competing writers interleave between chunks instead of queueing behind one lock set; a chunk that loses a race replays only its own id range instead of the whole statement. **Keyset, not fixed-width id stepping** — the CrowdStrike import is delete-then-insert per asset, so ids are sparse and `MAX(id)` runs far ahead of the row count, which would make blind stepping spend most iterations on empty ranges. The daily 03:00 `recomputeAllExceptedScheduled` now delegates to the same driver (its orphaned `selfProvider` removed), so the nightly pass stops reintroducing the hold. Chunking gives up atomicity, and that is argued rather than assumed: the operation is already `@Async`, its documented contract is already eventual ("rows stay visible until it lands", failures "non-fatal; standing sweeps will retry"), a mid-statement failure already left partial state, and readers evaluate `v.excepted = 0` per row without a cross-table snapshot — so no guarantee is lost, and a failure now leaves a converged *prefix* rather than nothing. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for the two integration tests that need single-step determinism on a tiny table, documented as not-for-production. Tests: `AsyncExceptionRecomputeChunkingTest` (5 cases pinning the traversal — sparse ids covered exactly once, half-open boundaries abutting without re-processing, no single range spanning the table) plus a `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest` case asserting the chunked statement assigns exactly what the atomic one does against a real database, with every flag pre-flipped so a skipped row cannot coincidentally match. Closes the `recomputeAll` lock-hold item open since the 2026-07-20 DB-pool work. OWASP: A01 reviewed — both new native queries bind parameters and take only primary-key boundaries from the preceding keyset read, on `@Async`/`@Scheduled` paths unreachable from any request.
53:- **Vulnerability SLA anchored to remediation availability (2026-08-24)** — `secman.vulnerability.use-patch-publication-date` now defaults to **true** (both `application.yml` and the `VulnerabilitySettings` data class, which had to be changed together — they disagreed, and a new `VulnerabilitySettingsDefaultTest` now pins both). Age is measured from when a **fix became available**, falling back to CrowdStrike detection age per row when no patch date is published. Rationale: detection age answers "how long have we known", which resets whenever a host is rebuilt or newly onboarded — a 2023 CVE on a month-old host read as a month old — while remediation age answers "how long could we have fixed this and did not" and does not reward re-imaging. This only became possible in the same change that made the field arrive at all: the CLI batch payload had been dropping `patchPublicationDate` entirely, so the flag was inert on the production import path, and the ad-hoc lookup path never populated the field either (its DTO construction set neither publication date, so "persist it on save" persisted null forever — both now use the shared `FalconTimestamps` extractors). Two consequences documented rather than discovered later: (1) **overdue counts jump** on the first import after the change, since a patch date is normally much earlier than the detection date, so expect an outsized notification run; (2) **it is a one-way door** — `first_seen_at` is preserved as `min(prior, new)` across re-imports (the property that stops a re-import resetting the SLA clock), so once an import writes the older patch date, setting the flag back to false does **not** restore the previous anchors. A genuine revert is `UPDATE vulnerability SET first_seen_at = NULL WHERE source = 'CROWDSTRIKE'` plus a full re-import with the flag off. `requirePatchPublicationDate` stays **false** and is pinned by test: despite the near-identical name it is a *filter*, not an anchor, and enabling it would drop every vulnerability with no published patch date — hiding risk rather than re-dating it. Nothing changes until the next import; existing rows keep their current anchors. `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix, `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`.
55:- **CrowdStrike date semantics: three dates untangled (2026-08-24)** — reported as "the import is wrong: a 2023 CVE cannot be only 226 days old". Investigation showed the arithmetic was right and the *meaning* was not, plus four real defects underneath. Falcon's `created_timestamp` is when Spotlight created that finding **on that host**, and it creates every finding against a package in one batch — so a host legitimately shows one identical age across dozens of CVEs. Confirmed on live data: `detectedAt` clusters (80 rows on one date, 60 on another) while the newly captured `cve.published_date` spreads across dozens. Also confirmed that a CVE's ID year is its *reservation* year — `CVE-2023-53178` in this estate has `published_date = 2025-09-15` — so "a 2023 CVE can't be 62 days old" was never a sound inference; the data to see that simply was not being captured. Fixes: (1) **`extractPatchPublicationDate` asked `cve.published_date` FIRST**, so the column named for a patch — and used as the SLA anchor when `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE=true` — usually held the CVE *disclosure* date, silently answering "how long since a fix existed?" with "how long since the CVE was published". Genuine remediation dates (`remediation.vendor_release_date`, `remediation.published_date`) now win; the CVE fields are kept as the **last** resort rather than removed, because `require-patch-publication-date` filters imports on this being non-null and narrowing it would have silently dropped rows — nothing that was non-null before becomes null. (2) **Timezone bug**: `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.parseDetectionTimestamp` (the ad-hoc lookup behind the reported screen) parsed `"2026-01-10T22:18:26Z"` by *stripping* the `Z` and handing the rest to `LocalDateTime.parse`, relabelling a UTC instant as system-local instead of converting it — a whole-day shift across midnight, since age is `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`. There were **four** copies of Falcon date parsing, one correct; all now delegate to one new `FalconTimestamps`, which also returns **null rather than `now()`** for an absent/unreadable date (defaulting to now reads as "detected today" = zero days = never overdue, a security miss dressed as a formatting fallback). (3) **The high-volume CLI batch payload dropped every date**: `/api/crowdstrike/servers/import` hand-built a map of `cveId`/`severity`/`affectedProduct`/`daysOpen` only, so `patchPublicationDate` was always null on the main import path and `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE` could never take effect there at all. It now also sends `detectedAt` and both publication dates, and the backend prefers `detectedAt` over re-deriving `importTimestamp − daysOpen` — the same cross-clock, twice-truncated reconstruction shape as the 2026-08-21 reconcile incident (`daysOpen` is still sent, and the reconstruction retained, so an older CLI keeps working). (4) Saving from the ad-hoc lookup dropped `patch_publication_date` entirely. New `cve_published_date` column (V259, nullable, not backfilled — the import is delete-then-insert, so rows acquire it on the next run) surfaced on the lookup page as a **CVE Published** column, with "Days Open" renamed to **Detected (days)** and tooltipped as "not the age of the CVE". Tests: `CrowdStrikeTimestampParsingTest` (8 cases pinning the timezone contract and unknown-stays-null), `FalconDateExtractionTest` (6 cases pinning the preference order *and* the deliberate CVE fallback). Three unrelated pre-existing failures that had been red on `main` were also fixed to get a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` — backend test sources did not compile at all), `InstalledProductListServiceTest` ×2 (mockk had no stub for a `countProductsByServer` call the service gained), and `VulnerabilityServicePreviewIntegrationTest` (reflection lookup missing the `includeInstallerFindings` parameter added by product classification). `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix.

59:- **CrowdStrike morning over-deletion fixes (2026-08-21 incident: 727,637 rows)** — every morning the post-import reconcile sweep deleted far too many vulnerability rows. Root cause from the prod log: the CLI's cutoff arrived timezone-skewed (>1h in the backend's future), the old guard fell back to `backendNow − 30min`, and because the import ran longer than 30 minutes the sweep judged everything the run imported in its first half-hour "stale" and deleted it — 727,637 rows in one statement, aborted=false. Fixes, layered: (1) **cutoff translation** — the CLI now sends `clientNow`; the backend measures the clock offset and translates `importStartedAt` into its own clock, and without `clientNow` a future cutoff **aborts** the sweep (delete nothing) instead of guessing; (2) **failure-aware sweep scope** — hosts whose Falcon Stage-2 batch failed/was truncated (`StreamingImportResult.failedHosts`) or whose backend POST/per-server transaction failed (`BatchStorageResult.failedHostnames`, `ImportStatisticsDto.failedHostnames`) are excluded from `queriedHosts`, since their un-refreshed rows were never fetched, not remediated; (3) **percentage brake** `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_MAX_DELETE_PERCENT` (default 20, 100 disables) over the resolved scope, fail-CLOSED on count errors — the zero-refresh brake only catches fully-empty runs; (4) **scoped per-host replace** — `importVulnerabilitiesForServer` no longer wipes every row on the asset: it deletes `source=CROWDSTRIKE` rows at the batch's `runSeverities` (new optional DTO field; source-only fallback for old callers), so MEDIUM/LOW and XLSX/nmap/manual rows survive, and a batch whose rows are ALL filtered out (blank CVE / missing patch date) skips the delete instead of committing delete-without-reinsert; (5) **stale-asset cleanup correctness** — rule A now vetoes assets with a recent `crowdStrikeAgentSeenAt` (a fully-patched host with a live sensor never refreshes `crowdStrikeLastImportedAt`), brake numerator and deletion use one shared cutoff and the same query, and the brake fails closed when the tracked-asset count is unavailable; (6) **observability** — reconcile audit columns on `crowdstrike_reconcile_job` (V257: queried/resolved/excluded counts, stale candidates, refreshed, dry_run), `--reconcile-dry-run` CLI flag, per-host replace logging at INFO, a `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_ABORTED` chat-notification event, and the MV refresh `triggered_by` insert no longer dies on over-length reasons (`.take(50)`, the log's second error). `scripts/import.sh` `--last-seen-days` regression 1→30 fixed (comment already said 30). `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` §CrowdStrike reconcile sweep.
60:- **Apple `container` database selection (`--db`)** — `secman-container.sh up` now takes `--db container|host|none` (plus `--db-host/--db-port/--db-name`; `--with-db`/`--no-db` are aliases for the first and last). `container`, the default, runs the in-container MariaDB and publishes it on :3306; `host` runs none and points the stack at the MariaDB already installed on the Mac; `none` leaves `DB_CONNECT` to `pass-cli`. `host` was previously not reachable at all: the egress policy carries only 80/443/22 to allow-set addresses, so port 3306 to the Mac was refused with no rule capable of permitting it. The entrypoint now settles the mode **before** the firewall is built, resolves the Mac's address (it is the container's default gateway, which only the container can see), and writes the result to `/run/secman-dev/db/env` — the single file the firewall, `devctl` and every login shell read, so the iptables rule and the JDBC URL cannot disagree, including after a `refresh-egress` that inherits none of the entrypoint's environment. The rule is deliberately narrow: one address, one port, outside the allow-set (which is only ever matched on 80/443/22), and the address must be private — a public one is refused unless `SECMAN_DEV_DB_ALLOW_PUBLIC=1`, so a convenience flag cannot become general 3306 egress. The choice is made effective rather than advisory: `/etc/profile.d/secman-dev.sh` exports the resulting `DB_CONNECT` (plus the throwaway `DB_USERNAME`/`DB_PASSWORD` in `container` mode only), and `scripts/startbackenddev.sh` now honours a preset `DB_CONNECT` and falls back to `pass://Test/SECMAN/DB_CONNECT` when it is unset — unchanged behaviour on a Mac. `devctl db status` / `secman-container.sh db` report the mode, the URL and a live reachability probe, and name the three silent failure modes of `--db host` in order (server not running, bound to 127.0.0.1 only, no grant for the container's subnet); `devctl db start` refuses outside `container` mode rather than raising a second server behind a URL that names a different one. Every value that reaches an iptables rule or a JDBC URL goes through a closed character allowlist at both ends (§A03). `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md` §Choosing the database.
62:- **Apple `container` shielded dev environment (macOS/Apple silicon)** — `./scripts/container/secman-container.sh` builds and drives one long-lived Apple `container` VM that carries the whole toolchain (Temurin 25, Gradle 9.7.0, Node 24, Go 1.24, uv/Python 3.13, MariaDB 11.4, nginx) plus Claude Code, Kimi CLI and `pass-cli`, so the agents run inside a shield rather than on the developer's Mac. Three properties are the point. **One host path**: the source tree passed with `--src` is the only bind mount; the Gradle/npm caches, the agent state, the Proton Pass session and the MariaDB data directory live in named volumes — invisible to macOS, faster than virtiofs, and no widening of the exposure the container exists to narrow. `up` refuses `/`, `/Users`, `$HOME` and friends rather than trusting the caller to notice. **Egress by iptables alone, deliberately without a proxy**: `OUTPUT` policy `DROP`, and the only ways out are loopback, replies on established connections, DNS to the resolvers in `/etc/resolv.conf`, and TCP on 80/443/22 to an address in the allow-set. That set is built from the allowlist's hostnames resolved to their A records, its address/CIDR literals, and GitHub's published ranges from `api.github.com/meta` (a service across that many prefixes cannot be covered by resolving a few names); it is held in an `ipset` where the kernel has one — a single hash lookup per packet and an atomic swap on refresh — and in a plain rule chain where it does not, both probed rather than assumed because Apple's kernel is trimmed. The consequence is stated rather than buried: filtering is by **address, not name**, so anything else answering on an allowlisted address is reachable, and an address that rotates out of DNS stays permitted until the next refresh while its replacement is not. The second half is handled by re-resolving every 30 minutes (`SECMAN_EGRESS_REFRESH_MINUTES`), without which a container left running overnight starts failing npm and Maven downloads for reasons that look nothing like a firewall; the first half is inherent to packet-layer filtering. Denials `REJECT` rather than `DROP` so a blocked tool fails immediately instead of hanging, and a rate-limited `LOG` rule plus the reject counter are the record of what was refused now that there is no proxy log. Three guards fail closed: the container **refuses to start** if a non-allowlisted host is reachable, an allowlist that renders to nothing is refused, and a resolution round in which more than half the names fail is refused as broken DNS rather than installed as a policy that reaches almost nothing. The allowlist covers both agents, Proton, GitHub, Gradle/Maven/Google/JetBrains/Adoptium, npm, Go, PyPI, Playwright, Debian/MariaDB apt, and the hosts the app itself calls (`endoflife.date`, `api.crowdstrike.com` and its regional siblings, `openrouter.ai`, `hooks.slack.com`, `api.telegram.org`, `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`); `SECMAN_HOST` and AWS's regional endpoints are deliberately absent, since neither can be guessed. **Ports 8080/4321/443/3306** come back to the Mac, with nginx terminating TLS on 443 in front of both services because the `secman_auth` cookie is `Secure` and a plain-HTTP dev origin produces a login that silently never persists. Apple-specific behaviour is handled rather than documented-around: the default kernel has no working nftables, so `iptables-legacy` is pinned explicitly (a silent fall-through to the nft backend would fail *open*); IPv6 is incomplete, so it is disabled and all `ip6tables` policies set to `DROP`; there is no privileged mode, so exactly `NET_ADMIN` + `NET_RAW` are added; `--publish` needs macOS 26 and the script says so on 15; options must precede the image name; macOS reserves ports below 1024 for root, so `up` probes and falls back to publishing `:443` on `8443`; virtiofs presents the Mac's uid (501, not 1000), so the entrypoint creates `dev` with the uid/gid that actually own `/workspace`. Because there is no proxy, nothing in the container needs `HTTP_PROXY` or `-Dhttps.proxyHost` — no JVM banner on every start, and no tool that quietly ignores those variables and behaves differently from the rest. `pass-cli` uses `PROTON_PASS_KEY_PROVIDER=file` (there is no OS keyring in the VM) with the session on a named volume, so `pass-cli login --interactive` is a one-time step and no Proton state ever touches the Mac's filesystem or Keychain. The `dev` user has no sudo: the firewall and its allowlist are root-owned, so an agent session cannot dismantle the shield it runs in. Values that reach SQL identifiers or an OpenSSL subject go through a closed character allowlist first (§A03), and `--allow-domain` entries clear a strict hostname/CIDR regex before they can reach an `iptables -d` argument. Full reference: `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md`.

Roles are resolved from the principal on every request and never cached on the device or baked into a token, so a demotion bites on the very next request with nothing to invalidate; principals are replace-on-push so roles can shrink, revocations stay additive so one is never undone by omission, and out-of-role / out-of-scope / nonexistent all answer an identical 403. **Sign-in layers three separate proofs**: Apple and Google ID tokens verified against their JWKS (RS256 pinned, iss/aud/exp and a single-use relay-issued nonce all checked — `aud` is what stops a token minted for another app); GitHub via the relay as a confidential OAuth client so the app never holds a GitHub credential; and a Secure Enclave P-256 key proving the device on every request. Binding is proof-of-possession throughout: the login nonce is bound to the device key and the binding request must carry that key's signature, so a captured ID token cannot register someone else's key. TLS on a selectable port in three modes — a **stdlib RFC 8555 ACME client** (Let's Encrypt, HTTP-01, renewal at 30 days), a file pair hot-reloaded on change, or plaintext for ALB termination behind an explicit `RELAY_PLAINTEXT_ACK=true`. The relay is **zero-third-party-dependency by contract** (its supply chain is the Go release plus this repo, and `go build` needs no module proxy), snapshot state is memory-only, and it fails closed on weak or placeholder secrets exactly as `JwtSigningValidator` does. 189 Go tests including a mock ACME CA that signs a real CSR and verifies every JWS, a mock OIDC issuer covering algorithm confusion / audience / issuer / expiry / nonce replay / key rotation, and end-to-end RBAC, revocation and staleness cases; a shared known-answer vector pins the ingest signature across Kotlin and Go so the two cannot drift silently. Adding a reportable event is a `NotificationEventType` constant plus one publish call — the settings APIs, both settings UIs and the dispatcher all derive from the enum, so nothing else changes. Adding a transport is one client plus one branch, with no publisher touched. **Subscriptions are rows, not columns**: `user_notification_subscription (user_id, channel, event_type)` — so a new event type or a whole new channel costs no migration, "who wants X over Slack" is a single indexed lookup on the dispatch path, and one user can route CrowdStrike to Slack and AWS imports to Telegram. Saving one channel's settings never disturbs the other's subscriptions (the replace is a per-channel diff, which also preserves `created_at` on kept rows). **Destination resolution.** Slack: personal incoming webhook → the user's channel via the workspace bot → the workspace default channel. Telegram: the user's chat ID is always required (Telegram addresses a conversation, not a person), with the token being the user's personal bot if set, otherwise the workspace bot — so a personal bot keeps working even when workspace delivery is switched off. - **Full `excepted` recompute chunked to stop multi-minute lock holds (2026-08-24)** — `VulnerabilityRepository.recomputeExceptedAll()` was a single `UPDATE vulnerability v JOIN asset a … SET v.excepted = CASE WHEN EXISTS(…)` **with no WHERE clause**. It took exclusive row locks on every `vulnerability` row (~1.8M in production) and, through its correlated subquery, read locks on `vulnerability_exception` — holding both for the entire 53–180s transaction. Every concurrent writer to either table then blocked until lock-wait-timeout: bulk exception delete/import, CrowdStrike imports, per-asset recomputes. `DeadlockRetry` absorbed the failure, which is exactly why it stayed hidden — but the *other* operation still paid the full timeout first, observed as ~40s per `delete_all_vulnerability_exceptions` in both E2E runs, contending with "Async full excepted recompute complete: 1824736 rows in 53481 ms". Fix: `AsyncExceptionRecompute.recomputeAllChunked` drives the recompute as bounded **keyset** chunks (`CHUNK_SIZE` 10,000) through the new `recomputeExceptedForIdRange(afterId, throughId)`, each in its own REQUIRES_NEW transaction with per-chunk `DeadlockRetry`. Lock hold per transaction drops from minutes to milliseconds, so competing writers interleave between chunks instead of queueing behind one lock set; a chunk that loses a race replays only its own id range instead of the whole statement. **Keyset, not fixed-width id stepping** — the CrowdStrike import is delete-then-insert per asset, so ids are sparse and `MAX(id)` runs far ahead of the row count, which would make blind stepping spend most iterations on empty ranges. The daily 03:00 `recomputeAllExceptedScheduled` now delegates to the same driver (its orphaned `selfProvider` removed), so the nightly pass stops reintroducing the hold. Chunking gives up atomicity, and that is argued rather than assumed: the operation is already `@Async`, its documented contract is already eventual ("rows stay visible until it lands", failures "non-fatal; standing sweeps will retry"), a mid-statement failure already left partial state, and readers evaluate `v.excepted = 0` per row without a cross-table snapshot — so no guarantee is lost, and a failure now leaves a converged *prefix* rather than nothing. `recomputeExceptedAll()` is retained for the two integration tests that need single-step determinism on a tiny table, documented as not-for-production. Tests: `AsyncExceptionRecomputeChunkingTest` (5 cases pinning the traversal — sparse ids covered exactly once, half-open boundaries abutting without re-processing, no single range spanning the table) plus a `ExceptedFlagSqlAgreementIntegrationTest` case asserting the chunked statement assigns exactly what the atomic one does against a real database, with every flag pre-flipped so a skipped row cannot coincidentally match. Closes the `recomputeAll` lock-hold item open since the 2026-07-20 DB-pool work. OWASP: A01 reviewed — both new native queries bind parameters and take only primary-key boundaries from the preceding keyset read, on `@Async`/`@Scheduled` paths unreachable from any request.

- **Vulnerability SLA anchored to remediation availability (2026-08-24)** — `secman.vulnerability.use-patch-publication-date` now defaults to **true** (both `application.yml` and the `VulnerabilitySettings` data class, which had to be changed together — they disagreed, and a new `VulnerabilitySettingsDefaultTest` now pins both). Age is measured from when a **fix became available**, falling back to CrowdStrike detection age per row when no patch date is published. Rationale: detection age answers "how long have we known", which resets whenever a host is rebuilt or newly onboarded — a 2023 CVE on a month-old host read as a month old — while remediation age answers "how long could we have fixed this and did not" and does not reward re-imaging. This only became possible in the same change that made the field arrive at all: the CLI batch payload had been dropping `patchPublicationDate` entirely, so the flag was inert on the production import path, and the ad-hoc lookup path never populated the field either (its DTO construction set neither publication date, so "persist it on save" persisted null forever — both now use the shared `FalconTimestamps` extractors). Two consequences documented rather than discovered later: (1) **overdue counts jump** on the first import after the change, since a patch date is normally much earlier than the detection date, so expect an outsized notification run; (2) **it is a one-way door** — `first_seen_at` is preserved as `min(prior, new)` across re-imports (the property that stops a re-import resetting the SLA clock), so once an import writes the older patch date, setting the flag back to false does **not** restore the previous anchors. A genuine revert is `UPDATE vulnerability SET first_seen_at = NULL WHERE source = 'CROWDSTRIKE'` plus a full re-import with the flag off. `requirePatchPublicationDate` stays **false** and is pinned by test: despite the near-identical name it is a *filter*, not an anchor, and enabling it would drop every vulnerability with no published patch date — hiding risk rather than re-dating it. Nothing changes until the next import; existing rows keep their current anchors. `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix, `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`.

- **CrowdStrike date semantics: three dates untangled (2026-08-24)** — reported as "the import is wrong: a 2023 CVE cannot be only 226 days old". Investigation showed the arithmetic was right and the *meaning* was not, plus four real defects underneath. Falcon's `created_timestamp` is when Spotlight created that finding **on that host**, and it creates every finding against a package in one batch — so a host legitimately shows one identical age across dozens of CVEs. Confirmed on live data: `detectedAt` clusters (80 rows on one date, 60 on another) while the newly captured `cve.published_date` spreads across dozens. Also confirmed that a CVE's ID year is its *reservation* year — `CVE-2023-53178` in this estate has `published_date = 2025-09-15` — so "a 2023 CVE can't be 62 days old" was never a sound inference; the data to see that simply was not being captured. Fixes: (1) **`extractPatchPublicationDate` asked `cve.published_date` FIRST**, so the column named for a patch — and used as the SLA anchor when `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE=true` — usually held the CVE *disclosure* date, silently answering "how long since a fix existed?" with "how long since the CVE was published". Genuine remediation dates (`remediation.vendor_release_date`, `remediation.published_date`) now win; the CVE fields are kept as the **last** resort rather than removed, because `require-patch-publication-date` filters imports on this being non-null and narrowing it would have silently dropped rows — nothing that was non-null before becomes null. (2) **Timezone bug**: `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.parseDetectionTimestamp` (the ad-hoc lookup behind the reported screen) parsed `"2026-01-10T22:18:26Z"` by *stripping* the `Z` and handing the rest to `LocalDateTime.parse`, relabelling a UTC instant as system-local instead of converting it — a whole-day shift across midnight, since age is `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between`. There were **four** copies of Falcon date parsing, one correct; all now delegate to one new `FalconTimestamps`, which also returns **null rather than `now()`** for an absent/unreadable date (defaulting to now reads as "detected today" = zero days = never overdue, a security miss dressed as a formatting fallback). (3) **The high-volume CLI batch payload dropped every date**: `/api/crowdstrike/servers/import` hand-built a map of `cveId`/`severity`/`affectedProduct`/`daysOpen` only, so `patchPublicationDate` was always null on the main import path and `VULN_USE_PATCH_PUBLICATION_DATE` could never take effect there at all. It now also sends `detectedAt` and both publication dates, and the backend prefers `detectedAt` over re-deriving `importTimestamp − daysOpen` — the same cross-clock, twice-truncated reconstruction shape as the 2026-08-21 reconcile incident (`daysOpen` is still sent, and the reconstruction retained, so an older CLI keeps working). (4) Saving from the ad-hoc lookup dropped `patch_publication_date` entirely. New `cve_published_date` column (V259, nullable, not backfilled — the import is delete-then-insert, so rows acquire it on the next run) surfaced on the lookup page as a **CVE Published** column, with "Days Open" renamed to **Detected (days)** and tooltipped as "not the age of the CVE". Tests: `CrowdStrikeTimestampParsingTest` (8 cases pinning the timezone contract and unknown-stays-null), `FalconDateExtractionTest` (6 cases pinning the preference order *and* the deliberate CVE fallback). Three unrelated pre-existing failures that had been red on `main` were also fixed to get a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` — backend test sources did not compile at all), `InstalledProductListServiceTest` ×2 (mockk had no stub for a `countProductsByServer` call the service gained), and `VulnerabilityServicePreviewIntegrationTest` (reflection lookup missing the `includeInstallerFindings` parameter added by product classification). `docs/CROWDSTRIKE_IMPORT.md` §Timestamp fix.

- **EOL mails carry the affected-systems table (2026-08-24)** — both EOL mail paths now embed the same table the product drilldown page shows, rendered by one new `EolFindingTableRenderer`: System, Type, Cloud account, **Cloud instance**, AD domain, Version, Release cycle, End of support, Status (plus Component for the owner notification, which spans many products; the broadcast is one product, so that column would be a constant). Previously the "Contact affected owners" broadcast (`/vulnerabilities/eol/products/{product}`) sent only the admin's free-text message with **no findings data at all**, and `secman send-eol-notifications` sent a 4-column Component/Version/Cycle/EOL table with no account, instance, domain, type or status — a recipient mapped to a whole AWS account could not tell which system or which account a row belonged to. Pieces: (1) **`cloudInstanceId` denormalized onto `eol_finding`** (V258, nullable, populated by `EolScanService` at both `ASSET_*` insertion sites exactly as `assetName`/`cloudAccountId`/`assetOwner` already are) and surfaced on `EolFindingResponse`, the page table and the CSV export so page, CSV and mail agree; deliberately **not backfilled** — the scan is delete-then-insert, so existing rows acquire it on the next `eol-sync` and read `-` until then; (2) **per-recipient scoping of the broadcast** — `EolBroadcastRecipientResolver.resolve` now returns `EolBroadcastRecipient(user, assetIds)` instead of `List<User>`, carrying the asset ids that made each user a recipient, and `EmailBroadcastService` renders only those rows into that recipient's copy. That linkage (owner, manual creator, scan uploader, AWS-account mapping, AD-domain mapping) is criteria 3/4/5/6/8 of §Unified Asset Access, hence provably a subset of what the recipient may already see (§A01) at **zero extra access queries** and with no way to drift from the rule that produced the recipient; sending one shared table would have disclosed other tenants' hostnames and account ids to every owner on the list. Manually-entered Cc addresses ride along on the owner's message and see that owner's rows only; (3) **bounded output** — rows and count are both taken at the query (`findByComponentNameForAssets` page of 200 + `countByComponentNameForAssets`), never fetched whole and sliced in Kotlin (§A04), and the remainder is disclosed in the table footer rather than silently truncated; (4) **one escaping sink** — the renderer escapes at assembly and strips CR/LF from the text part, replacing `EolNotificationService`'s private `escapeHtml`/`sanitizeForText` (which also escaped *before* truncating, so a 512-char cut could split an entity); the table is generated server-side at send time and never passes `EmailBroadcastService.sanitizeBroadcastHtml`, whose safelist strips every attribute except `a[href|title]` and would have removed the inline styles mail clients need. The compose modal now says the table is appended automatically and is scoped per recipient. Unrelated pre-existing breakage fixed to reach a green build: `ResponseControllerAccessControlTest` failed to compile on `main` (four `Cannot infer type for type parameter 'O'` on single-arg `exchange(...)`), so backend test sources did not build at all. `docs/EOL.md` §5.1.

- **CrowdStrike morning over-deletion fixes (2026-08-21 incident: 727,637 rows)** — every morning the post-import reconcile sweep deleted far too many vulnerability rows. Root cause from the prod log: the CLI's cutoff arrived timezone-skewed (>1h in the backend's future), the old guard fell back to `backendNow − 30min`, and because the import ran longer than 30 minutes the sweep judged everything the run imported in its first half-hour "stale" and deleted it — 727,637 rows in one statement, aborted=false. Fixes, layered: (1) **cutoff translation** — the CLI now sends `clientNow`; the backend measures the clock offset and translates `importStartedAt` into its own clock, and without `clientNow` a future cutoff **aborts** the sweep (delete nothing) instead of guessing; (2) **failure-aware sweep scope** — hosts whose Falcon Stage-2 batch failed/was truncated (`StreamingImportResult.failedHosts`) or whose backend POST/per-server transaction failed (`BatchStorageResult.failedHostnames`, `ImportStatisticsDto.failedHostnames`) are excluded from `queriedHosts`, since their un-refreshed rows were never fetched, not remediated; (3) **percentage brake** `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_MAX_DELETE_PERCENT` (default 20, 100 disables) over the resolved scope, fail-CLOSED on count errors — the zero-refresh brake only catches fully-empty runs; (4) **scoped per-host replace** — `importVulnerabilitiesForServer` no longer wipes every row on the asset: it deletes `source=CROWDSTRIKE` rows at the batch's `runSeverities` (new optional DTO field; source-only fallback for old callers), so MEDIUM/LOW and XLSX/nmap/manual rows survive, and a batch whose rows are ALL filtered out (blank CVE / missing patch date) skips the delete instead of committing delete-without-reinsert; (5) **stale-asset cleanup correctness** — rule A now vetoes assets with a recent `crowdStrikeAgentSeenAt` (a fully-patched host with a live sensor never refreshes `crowdStrikeLastImportedAt`), brake numerator and deletion use one shared cutoff and the same query, and the brake fails closed when the tracked-asset count is unavailable; (6) **observability** — reconcile audit columns on `crowdstrike_reconcile_job` (V257: queried/resolved/excluded counts, stale candidates, refreshed, dry_run), `--reconcile-dry-run` CLI flag, per-host replace logging at INFO, a `CROWDSTRIKE_RECONCILE_ABORTED` chat-notification event, and the MV refresh `triggered_by` insert no longer dies on over-length reasons (`.take(50)`, the log's second error). `scripts/import.sh` `--last-seen-days` regression 1→30 fixed (comment already said 30). `docs/ENVIRONMENT.md` §CrowdStrike reconcile sweep.
- **Apple `container` database selection (`--db`)** — `secman-container.sh up` now takes `--db container|host|none` (plus `--db-host/--db-port/--db-name`; `--with-db`/`--no-db` are aliases for the first and last). `container`, the default, runs the in-container MariaDB and publishes it on :3306; `host` runs none and points the stack at the MariaDB already installed on the Mac; `none` leaves `DB_CONNECT` to `pass-cli`. `host` was previously not reachable at all: the egress policy carries only 80/443/22 to allow-set addresses, so port 3306 to the Mac was refused with no rule capable of permitting it. The entrypoint now settles the mode **before** the firewall is built, resolves the Mac's address (it is the container's default gateway, which only the container can see), and writes the result to `/run/secman-dev/db/env` — the single file the firewall, `devctl` and every login shell read, so the iptables rule and the JDBC URL cannot disagree, including after a `refresh-egress` that inherits none of the entrypoint's environment. The rule is deliberately narrow: one address, one port, outside the allow-set (which is only ever matched on 80/443/22), and the address must be private — a public one is refused unless `SECMAN_DEV_DB_ALLOW_PUBLIC=1`, so a convenience flag cannot become general 3306 egress. The choice is made effective rather than advisory: `/etc/profile.d/secman-dev.sh` exports the resulting `DB_CONNECT` (plus the throwaway `DB_USERNAME`/`DB_PASSWORD` in `container` mode only), and `scripts/startbackenddev.sh` now honours a preset `DB_CONNECT` and falls back to `pass://Test/SECMAN/DB_CONNECT` when it is unset — unchanged behaviour on a Mac. `devctl db status` / `secman-container.sh db` report the mode, the URL and a live reachability probe, and name the three silent failure modes of `--db host` in order (server not running, bound to 127.0.0.1 only, no grant for the container's subnet); `devctl db start` refuses outside `container` mode rather than raising a second server behind a URL that names a different one. Every value that reaches an iptables rule or a JDBC URL goes through a closed character allowlist at both ends (§A03). `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md` §Choosing the database.

- **Apple `container` shielded dev environment (macOS/Apple silicon)** — `./scripts/container/secman-container.sh` builds and drives one long-lived Apple `container` VM that carries the whole toolchain (Temurin 25, Gradle 9.7.0, Node 24, Go 1.24, uv/Python 3.13, MariaDB 11.4, nginx) plus Claude Code, Kimi CLI and `pass-cli`, so the agents run inside a shield rather than on the developer's Mac. Three properties are the point. **One host path**: the source tree passed with `--src` is the only bind mount; the Gradle/npm caches, the agent state, the Proton Pass session and the MariaDB data directory live in named volumes — invisible to macOS, faster than virtiofs, and no widening of the exposure the container exists to narrow. `up` refuses `/`, `/Users`, `$HOME` and friends rather than trusting the caller to notice. **Egress by iptables alone, deliberately without a proxy**: `OUTPUT` policy `DROP`, and the only ways out are loopback, replies on established connections, DNS to the resolvers in `/etc/resolv.conf`, and TCP on 80/443/22 to an address in the allow-set. That set is built from the allowlist's hostnames resolved to their A records, its address/CIDR literals, and GitHub's published ranges from `api.github.com/meta` (a service across that many prefixes cannot be covered by resolving a few names); it is held in an `ipset` where the kernel has one — a single hash lookup per packet and an atomic swap on refresh — and in a plain rule chain where it does not, both probed rather than assumed because Apple's kernel is trimmed. The consequence is stated rather than buried: filtering is by **address, not name**, so anything else answering on an allowlisted address is reachable, and an address that rotates out of DNS stays permitted until the next refresh while its replacement is not. The second half is handled by re-resolving every 30 minutes (`SECMAN_EGRESS_REFRESH_MINUTES`), without which a container left running overnight starts failing npm and Maven downloads for reasons that look nothing like a firewall; the first half is inherent to packet-layer filtering. Denials `REJECT` rather than `DROP` so a blocked tool fails immediately instead of hanging, and a rate-limited `LOG` rule plus the reject counter are the record of what was refused now that there is no proxy log. Three guards fail closed: the container **refuses to start** if a non-allowlisted host is reachable, an allowlist that renders to nothing is refused, and a resolution round in which more than half the names fail is refused as broken DNS rather than installed as a policy that reaches almost nothing. The allowlist covers both agents, Proton, GitHub, Gradle/Maven/Google/JetBrains/Adoptium, npm, Go, PyPI, Playwright, Debian/MariaDB apt, and the hosts the app itself calls (`endoflife.date`, `api.crowdstrike.com` and its regional siblings, `openrouter.ai`, `hooks.slack.com`, `api.telegram.org`, `acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org`); `SECMAN_HOST` and AWS's regional endpoints are deliberately absent, since neither can be guessed. **Ports 8080/4321/443/3306** come back to the Mac, with nginx terminating TLS on 443 in front of both services because the `secman_auth` cookie is `Secure` and a plain-HTTP dev origin produces a login that silently never persists. Apple-specific behaviour is handled rather than documented-around: the default kernel has no working nftables, so `iptables-legacy` is pinned explicitly (a silent fall-through to the nft backend would fail *open*); IPv6 is incomplete, so it is disabled and all `ip6tables` policies set to `DROP`; there is no privileged mode, so exactly `NET_ADMIN` + `NET_RAW` are added; `--publish` needs macOS 26 and the script says so on 15; options must precede the image name; macOS reserves ports below 1024 for root, so `up` probes and falls back to publishing `:443` on `8443`; virtiofs presents the Mac's uid (501, not 1000), so the entrypoint creates `dev` with the uid/gid that actually own `/workspace`. Because there is no proxy, nothing in the container needs `HTTP_PROXY` or `-Dhttps.proxyHost` — no JVM banner on every start, and no tool that quietly ignores those variables and behaves differently from the rest. `pass-cli` uses `PROTON_PASS_KEY_PROVIDER=file` (there is no OS keyring in the VM) with the session on a named volume, so `pass-cli login --interactive` is a one-time step and no Proton state ever touches the Mac's filesystem or Keychain. The `dev` user has no sudo: the firewall and its allowlist are root-owned, so an agent session cannot dismantle the shield it runs in. Values that reach SQL identifiers or an OpenSSL subject go through a closed character allowlist first (§A03), and `--allow-domain` entries clear a strict hostname/CIDR regex before they can reach an `iptables -d` argument. Full reference: `docs/APPLE_CONTAINER_DEV.md`.

- **Vulnerability export IP addresses** — the Excel export has carried an `IP` column all along (`ExportJobService.createHeaderRow`, column 1, fed from `Asset.ip`), but it came out blank for CrowdStrike-imported assets because the ingest side never asked CrowdStrike for the IP. Spotlight returns `local_ip` — together with `machine_domain`, `instance_id`, `service_provider_account_id` and `os_version` — inside a `host_info` object that is omitted from the response unless `facet=host_info` is requested, and all four Spotlight vulnerability queries (`CrowdStrikeApiClientImpl.queryAllVulnerabilitiesBulk`, `queryBatchVulnerabilities`, `querySpotlightApi`, and the backend's `CrowdStrikeVulnerabilityService.queryCrowdStrikeApi`) asked only for `facet=cve`. - **Public standard download: any standard, any release, over a plain GET** — the unauthenticated `/requirements/download` page could export the whole corpus or one use case, but not a *standard*, and there was no way to ask for "the latest released version of the IT/OT Security standard" from a script. `GET /api/requirements/export/{docx,xlsx}` now take four optional query parameters — `standard` (exact name, case-insensitive), `standardId` (wins if both given), `release` (`latest`, or an exact version) and the pre-existing `releaseId` — all `IS_ANONYMOUS`, matching the four public export endpoints that already existed. - **AWS account risk assessment: validation pass, three defects closed** — a review of the opt-in auto-start path (`manage-user-mappings import --start-risk-assessment --risk-usecase <name>`, mirrored on `import-s3`, REST `POST /api/user-mappings/bulk` and MCP `import_user_mappings`) confirmed the contract holds — the flag is off by default, the use case comes from a flag, and without the flag the import runs exactly as before — and turned up three things that did not. **(1) The deadline had no upper bound.** `validateStartRequest` rejected `< 1` and nothing else, so `--risk-deadline-days 2147483647` produced an `endDate` outside the SQL `DATE` range; because assessments are started *after* the mapping import commits, that surfaced as a per-account error with the mappings already persisted, and a merely absurd value like `100000` (one keystroke from `1000`) was accepted silently into an assessment the reminder scheduler — which looks two days ahead — would never wake up for. Now `MAX_DEADLINE_DAYS = 3650`, checked in `validateStartRequest` so REST and MCP share it, mirrored as `UserMappingCliService.MAX_RISK_DEADLINE_DAYS` in both CLI commands (the CLI is a separate Gradle module and cannot reference the backend constant; `ImportCommandTest` pins the two together), and clamped rather than thrown in `startAssessmentsForNewAccounts` for a direct service call, since that runs past the commit point. The MCP input schema now advertises `maximum`. **(2) The idempotent skip was reported as a failure.** When a pair already had an open assessment, `createAssessment` returned "an open risk assessment (id=…) already exists" in `AccountRiskAssessmentInfo.error`, so both CLI commands printed it as ❌/FAILED, counted it in `riskAssessmentFailures` and exited 1 — for an outcome that is the feature working correctly. The DTO gained `skipped` / `skipReason` (and the MCP result the same two fields), `error` stays null, and both CLIs render it as a skip that does not affect the exit code. **Load-bearing detail:** the owner-notification gate used to rely on `error != null` to suppress the duplicate mail, so it now tests `!info.skipped` as well — otherwise every re-import would re-notify. The path is only reachable when the mapping row was deleted and the account is imported again while its assessment is still open; a plain re-import never reaches the guard, because the account is no longer new. **(3) The email boundary was too loose.** `UserMappingService.emailRegex` was `^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$`, and `[^@]` matches control characters, spaces and commas — so `alice\r\nBcc: x@evil.com` passed validation. That address is not just a row: it becomes the SMTP recipient of the start and reminder mails, it is interpolated into log lines (`Started risk assessment … owner={}`), and it is written into the assessment's `notes`. The pattern now excludes whitespace and `, ; : < > " \` (a comma makes `InternetAddress.parse` split one recipient into two; a CR/LF reaches a log line), length is capped at the 255-char column width so an overlong address fails as one ordinary row error instead of a post-commit `DataException`, and the three "invalid …" messages that echo the rejected value run it through `sanitizeForMessage` (control characters → `?`, truncated at 80). - **Generic chat notifications (Slack + Telegram), configurable per user** — SecMan can now message a user in Slack and/or Telegram when a reportable event completes, with each user choosing their own destination and, independently per channel, which events they want. Two events ship: `CROWDSTRIKE_REPORT_COMPLETED` ("New CrowdStrike report completed") and `AWS_ACCOUNT_IMPORT_COMPLETED` ("New AWS account import completed"). **Architecture is transport- and event-agnostic on purpose.** Publishers know nothing about chat: they publish a `ChatNotificationEvent` (event type, title, summary, label/value fields) and `ChatNotificationEventListener` (`@EventListener @Async`) hands it to `ChatNotificationService`, which resolves subscribers, destinations and rendering. Adding a reportable event is a `NotificationEventType` constant plus one publish call — the settings APIs, both settings UIs and the dispatcher all derive from the enum, so nothing else changes. Adding a transport is one client plus one branch, with no publisher touched. **Subscriptions are rows, not columns**: `user_notification_subscription (user_id, channel, event_type)` — so a new event type or a whole new channel costs no migration, "who wants X over Slack" is a single indexed lookup on the dispatch path, and one user can route CrowdStrike to Slack and AWS imports to Telegram. Saving one channel's settings never disturbs the other's subscriptions (the replace is a per-channel diff, which also preserves `created_at` on kept rows). **Destination resolution.** Slack: personal incoming webhook → the user's channel via the workspace bot → the workspace default channel. Telegram: the user's chat ID is always required (Telegram addresses a conversation, not a person), with the token being the user's personal bot if set, otherwise the workspace bot — so a personal bot keeps working even when workspace delivery is switched off. A subscriber who is enabled but has nowhere to send is recorded as `SKIPPED`, not `FAILED`; the UI resolves the same precedence client-side (`resolveSlackDestination` / `resolveTelegramDestination`) and warns *before* save rather than letting someone tick boxes that silently deliver nothing. **Where the events fire.** AWS account imports complete in one call, so `UserMappingBulkImportService.execute` (REST bulk + MCP, tagged with the calling entry point) and both `ImportController` upload paths publish immediately, after the import has committed and last among the post-commit side effects. CrowdStrike has no such point: a full CLI import arrives as ~94 sub-batch requests across 3 concurrent workers with no well-defined last batch, so `ImportCompletionNotifier` accumulates the run's totals in memory and a `@Scheduled` sweep publishes exactly **one** event once `SECMAN_CHAT_CROWDSTRIKE_QUIET_PERIOD_SECONDS` (180s) have passed with no activity — the same server-side debounce shape, and for the same reason, as `MaterializedViewRefreshService.requestDeferredRefresh`, and it keeps working for older CLI versions, the `/api/crowdstrike/vulnerabilities/save` path and manual callers. **Security.** The per-user Slack webhook URL is the only place in the platform where a non-admin supplies a URL the backend then fetches, so it is checked against a fixed `https://hooks.slack.com/` prefix *and* parsed-host equality (a prefix match alone passes `https://hooks.slack.com.evil.example/...`), rejects userinfo, non-default ports and non-https, and redirects are never followed. The Telegram bot token is interpolated into the request URL **path** (`/bot<token>/sendMessage`), so its `<digits>:<secret>` shape is validated as a security control — a token containing `/` or `..` would otherwise redirect the request to another path on the API host. Slack channels and Telegram chat IDs are validated against conservative character classes. Every credential (both workspace bot tokens, each user's webhook URL and personal bot token) is stored through `EncryptedStringConverter`, never returned by any API — the responses report only `…Configured: true/false` — and the `***HIDDEN***` mask is accepted back to mean "keep the stored value", with `''` meaning "clear it". Slack messages escape Slack's three reserved characters so an imported hostname cannot inject a fake link; Telegram messages are sent with **no** `parse_mode`, deliberately, because MarkdownV2 reserves 18 characters and rejects the whole message on one unescaped occurrence. Every route acts on the caller's own settings — the user id comes from the token and is never read from the body. Dispatch is deliberately **not** `@Transactional`: it performs outbound HTTP with a multi-second timeout per recipient, and wrapping it would pin a pooled DB connection for the whole fan-out (the 2026-07-21 HikariCP starvation incident was exactly that shape). Delivery is per-recipient and per-channel isolated: one bad webhook never stops another user's message, one channel's outage never suppresses the other, and nothing can propagate back into the import that published the event. **New endpoints**: `GET /api/notification-events` (catalogue, authenticated); `GET/PUT /api/slack/settings`, `POST /api/slack/settings/test`, `GET/PUT /api/telegram/settings`, `POST /api/telegram/settings/test` (authenticated, self-scoped); `GET/PUT /api/slack/config`, `POST /api/slack/config/test`, `GET/PUT /api/telegram/config` (ADMIN). No Telegram workspace test endpoint — a bot token addresses no conversation on its own, so a meaningful test needs a chat ID and lives on the user page. **UI**: `/chat-notifications` (all users, linked from the account dropdown) with independent Slack and Telegram cards sharing a `NotificationEventSelector` and `ChatDeliveryStatusLine`; `/admin/chat-config` (ADMIN, linked under System Configuration). **Schema**: `V252__chat_notifications.sql` adds `slack_config`, `telegram_config`, `user_slack_settings`, `user_telegram_settings`, `user_notification_subscription`. **Tests**: `SlackClientTest` and `TelegramClientTest` (the URL/token/channel/chat-id allowlists, including that a rejected value never reaches the network), `ChatMessageRendererTest` (both flavours + Slack escaping), `ChatNotificationServiceTest` (24 cases: subscription filtering, both destination precedence chains, skipped-vs-failed, per-recipient and per-channel isolation, outcome recording), `ImportCompletionNotifierTest` (94 sub-batches → one event with correct totals, nothing published mid-import, totals reset between runs, the account-ID list cap), and `chatValidation.test.ts` on the frontend (17 cases mirroring the backend validators and both destination resolvers). On merging main, the newly-binding §OWASP Top 10 section prompted a re-read of the diff against A01–A10 and turned up one real gap: provider exception text was logged and persisted into `last_delivery_error` verbatim, and several JDK `HttpClient` exceptions echo the request URI — which for Telegram *contains the bot token* and for a Slack webhook *is* the credential. Both clients now scrub the secret out of any error before it is logged or stored (A02: no credential may reach a value that lands in a log), covered by a test per client. Migration renumbered `V251` → `V252__chat_notifications.sql`, since main landed its own `V251__user_profile_picture.sql` — two files sharing a Flyway version fails the migration at boot. **OWASP: A01/A02/A03/A04/A05/A08/A09/A10 touched — clean.** **Not verified in this environment**: `./gradlew build` and `./scripts/startbackenddev.sh` could not run — the session's egress policy blocks `services.gradle.org` and `repo1.maven.org`, and no Gradle 9.7.0 distribution or dependency cache is present — so the backend is compile-unverified and CLAUDE.md principle 5 and the principle-7 E2E gates are undischarged. The frontend gates did run: `npm ci && npm run build` clean, `npm test` 76 passing, and `@astrojs/check` reports zero type errors in any new or changed file (the 10 it finds are all pre-existing in untouched files).

- **Profile picture management (upload / crop / replace / remove)** — any authenticated user can now set an avatar from `/profile`; it replaces the generic `bi-person-circle` icon beside their name in the header dropdown. Scope is deliberately **own picture only** — there are no ADMIN-manages-others endpoints, and none of the three routes (`GET`/`POST`/`DELETE /api/users/profile/picture`, all on the existing `UserProfileController`) takes a user identifier, so the subject is always `authentication.name` and cross-user access is *structurally* impossible rather than merely checked. The paths are two literal segments, so they cannot collide with the ADMIN-gated single-segment `@Get("/{id}")` on `UserController`, which shares the `/api/users` prefix. **Bytes are stored in the database but never as uploaded**: `ProfilePictureService` validates cheapest-first (size cap → MIME allowlist → filename-extension/MIME agreement → magic bytes → header-only dimensions → the `ImageReader`'s own `formatName`) and then decodes, centre-crops to a square, scales to 256 px and re-encodes. That round trip — not the magic-byte sniff — is the control that actually matters: it destroys polyglot payloads (a valid PNG with `<script>` appended still decodes as a PNG and would pass any header check) and strips EXIF/GPS metadata, verified by a dedicated test. The **dimension probe runs before `reader.read(0)`**, so a 2 MB PNG cannot decode into a multi-gigabyte `BufferedImage` and trip `-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError` on the 1 GB heap; without that guard the endpoint would be a single-request kill switch. WEBP is deliberately **absent** from the allowlist (the JDK has no WEBP reader, so accepting it would mean storing bytes that were never decoded) — this costs nothing in practice because the frontend cropper exports its canvas as PNG, so WEBP/HEIC sources still work end to end. SVG is rejected three independent ways: not in the allowlist, `.svg` already in `SecurityService.DANGEROUS_EXTENSIONS`, and no SVG `ImageReader` exists. Only the JDK is used (`javax.imageio`/`java.awt.image`); `-Djava.awt.headless=true` was pinned in `applicationDefaultJvmArgs`. Storage is a **side table** `user_profile_picture` (V251, 1:1, `ON DELETE CASCADE`), not a column on `users`: `users` is loaded on every authenticated request and **`@Basic(fetch = LAZY)` on a `@Lob` is inert without Hibernate bytecode enhancement, which this build does not enable** — a blob column on `users` would therefore be fetched eagerly, every time. For the same reason the hot metadata paths use the blob-free projection `findUpdatedAtByUserId`, never `findByUserId`. `UserProfileDto` and `AuthController.StatusResponse` gained `hasProfilePicture` + `profilePictureUpdatedAt` (both defaulted, so purely additive); `LoginResponse` and the four `sessionStorage['user']` writers were deliberately **left alone** — `auth-init.ts` and `login/success.astro` store the whole `/api/auth/status` response verbatim and `Login.tsx` redirects immediately into a fresh status call, so they pick the fields up for free. **The header `<img>` is gated on `hasProfilePicture` rather than rendered unconditionally with an `onError` fallback**: `tests/js-error-scanner.mjs` records any status ≥ 400 as a failure, so an unconditional request would 404 on every page for every user without a picture and fail the `/e2ejs` merge gate. For the same reason `DELETE` returns 204 unconditionally instead of 404 when nothing is set. Frontend: new `ProfilePictureCard.tsx` (preview, drag & drop, and a hand-rolled canvas crop/zoom step — pointer-drag to pan, wheel/slider to zoom, exported at 512 px via `canvas.toBlob`; no cropping library added, the repo carries none), mounted as the first card on `/profile` and seeded from the profile fetch that already ran, so no extra metadata request. After a save or removal it patches `window.currentUser`/`sessionStorage` and re-dispatches the **existing** `userLoaded` event that `Header.tsx` already listens for, so the navbar avatar updates without a reload. Serving uses `inline` disposition — the first such endpoint in the repo — which is safe only because the `Content-Type` served is the stored, service-chosen value and never the client's declared one, and the `Content-Disposition` filename is synthesized from a `Long` and a constant so no user input reaches a response header. Upload, removal **and rejection** are audit-logged (a stream of `PROFILE_PICTURE_UPLOAD_REJECTED` is exactly the signal wanted when someone probes with polyglots). Tests: `ProfilePictureServiceTest` (19 cases incl. the polyglot-stripping and bomb-guard proofs), `UserProfilePictureIntegrationTest` (happy path, replace-updates-one-row, every rejection branch, 401 on all three routes, idempotent delete, cross-user isolation, cascade).
